title: Self-RAG Overview
text: Self-RAG is a retrieval-augmented generation framework that teaches a language model to decide when to retrieve passages and to critique whether its answer is relevant, supported, and useful. It uses reflection tokens to control and assess retrieval decisions at inference time.

title: PubMedQA Dataset
text: PubMedQA is a biomedical question answering dataset built from PubMed abstracts. Each example includes a yes/no/maybe question, a biomedical context passage, and a long-form rationale. It can be used as a domain adaptation corpus for biomedical retrieval-augmented generation experiments.

title: PopQA Benchmark
text: PopQA is an open-domain question answering benchmark commonly used to evaluate factual recall and retrieval-augmented generation systems. It contains questions about popular entities with varying degrees of popularity.

title: Self-RAG Reflection Tokens
text: Self-RAG uses four categories of reflection tokens. The retrieve token decides whether external retrieval is needed. The isREL token assesses whether a retrieved passage is relevant. The isSUP token judges whether the answer is supported by the passage. The isUSE token rates the utility of the final answer on a scale from 1 to 5.

title: Naive RAG vs Self-RAG
text: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation always retrieves passages for every query regardless of whether retrieval is helpful. Self-RAG improves on this by making retrieval conditional: it only retrieves when the model predicts that evidence is needed. After retrieval, it scores relevance and support for each passage and selects the best-grounded candidate answer.

title: BM25 Sparse Retrieval
text: BM25 is a probabilistic sparse retrieval model that scores documents based on term frequency and inverse document frequency with document length normalization. It is widely used as a strong baseline in information retrieval and is often combined with dense retrieval in hybrid systems to capture both lexical and semantic similarity.

title: Hybrid Dense and Sparse Retrieval
text: Hybrid retrieval combines dense vector similarity with sparse BM25 term matching to improve passage ranking. Dense retrieval captures semantic similarity using embedding vectors, while sparse retrieval captures lexical overlap. The final score is a weighted combination of both components. Hybrid retrieval systems consistently outperform either method alone on open-domain QA benchmarks.

title: LoRA Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
text: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that inserts trainable low-rank matrices into the attention layers of a frozen pretrained model. Only the small adapter parameters are updated during training, which greatly reduces memory usage and compute cost. LoRA is widely used to adapt large language models to new tasks or domains without full model fine-tuning.

title: LLaMA 2 Architecture
text: LLaMA 2 is an open foundation language model from Meta AI using a transformer decoder with grouped query attention and rotary positional embeddings. The 7B parameter variant can be loaded on a single 24GB GPU. Self-RAG is trained on LLaMA 2 using supervised fine-tuning with reflection token supervision from a critic model.

title: Hallucination in Language Models
text: Hallucination refers to the generation of factually incorrect or unsupported statements by language models. It is a key challenge in knowledge-intensive tasks such as question answering and summarization. Retrieval-augmented generation helps reduce hallucinations by grounding generation in external evidence. Self-RAG further reduces hallucinations by explicitly verifying whether each generated answer is supported by retrieved passages.

title: Biomedical Question Answering
text: Biomedical question answering requires accurate, evidence-grounded responses to clinical and research questions. Standard language models may generate incorrect medical facts. Retrieval-augmented systems that retrieve from biomedical corpora such as PubMed are better suited for this domain. Adapting Self-RAG to biomedical QA involves building a domain-specific index and evaluating yes/no/maybe label accuracy.

title: 4-bit Quantization for LLMs
text: 4-bit quantization using the BitsAndBytes library reduces the memory footprint of large language models by storing weights in 4 bits instead of 16 bits. NF4 format with double quantization allows a 7B parameter model to fit in approximately 6-8 GB of GPU memory while preserving inference quality. The compute dtype is kept at float16 for numerical stability.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval
text: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) uses dual encoder neural networks to embed queries and passages into a shared dense vector space. Retrieval is performed by finding nearest neighbor vectors using dot product similarity. DPR achieves strong recall on open-domain QA benchmarks and is used as a backbone retriever in many retrieval-augmented generation systems.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines a pretrained language model with a retrieval module to ground generation in external knowledge. Given a query, a retriever finds relevant passages from a large corpus, and the generator conditions its output on both the query and retrieved passages. RAG achieves strong performance on open-domain question answering and fact verification tasks.

title: Self-RAG Inference Pipeline
text: At inference time, Self-RAG runs a segment-level generation process. For each query segment, the model first decides whether to retrieve. If retrieval is triggered, it fetches top-k passages and generates candidate answers conditioned on each passage. Each candidate receives a composite score based on relevance, support, and utility tokens. The highest-scoring candidate is returned as the final answer.
